new.title: Settle into Chez Jules on the market square
new.desc: The brasserie at 8 Place Dalton bills itself as the Boulogne brasserie par excellence since 1895 and carries the Maître Restaurateur title. The menu leans on Opal Coast fish and seafood platters, alongside tête de veau and a welsh boulonnais, with bread, terrines and desserts made in the kitchen.
new.tip: It is open every day and serves through the afternoon, which is rare in town. Ask for a terrace table on market mornings, when the stalls set up right in front.

new.title: Treat yourself to fish at La Matelote
new.desc: This family-run house on Boulevard Sainte-Beuve, across from Nausicaá, takes its name from the fisherman's wife, said to know better than anyone how to cook the catch. The Michelin Guide lists it for seafood prepared with classic technique, and a soufflé is the signature dish.
new.tip: It serves dinner only on Thursdays and both services on other days. Book ahead for weekends and holiday periods.

new.title: Spot Napoleon's sea fort off Le Portel beach
new.desc: Fort de l'Heurt was ordered by Napoleon in 1803, after the Peace of Amiens broke down, to guard the southern end of the anchorage where his invasion flotilla lay. It was in service by July 1804 despite storms and British attacks, and part of it collapsed in a storm in November 1998.
new.tip: Look for it from the Le Portel seafront at low tide, when the rock it stands on is uncovered. The ruin is fragile, so admire it from the sand rather than climbing it.

new.title: Tour Fort de la Crèche with its volunteers
new.desc: This coastal battery of the Séré de Rivières system went up around 1879 on the headland between Boulogne and Wimereux. The German navy took it over in 1940 and built it into the Atlantic Wall, and Canadian troops of the Queen's Own Rifles captured it in September 1944. An association has been restoring it since 2002.
new.tip: Visits are guided and only run on set dates, so check the calendar on the association's website first. On a clear day the view takes in the Baie Saint-Jean and the English coast.

new.title: Carve a beet lantern for the Fête des Guénels
new.desc: In the days before Christmas, children of the Boulonnais hollow out sugar beets, carve faces in them and light them from inside with a candle. These lanterns are called guénels, and their bearers sing a traditional song in exchange for sweets. Boulogne holds a carving contest in the town centre, with beets handed out by the organisers.
new.tip: The date moves from year to year, so look at the town's Christmas programme. The contest is open to everyone and every entrant leaves with a prize.

new.title: Eat the day's landing at Aux Pêcheurs d'Étaples
new.desc: On the Canche quay at Étaples, this seafood restaurant serves what the town's fishing fleet brings in. Gault&Millau picks it out for very fresh fish landed directly, with dishes such as bouillabaisse étaploise and skate grenobloise, and set menus named Matelot, Officier and Major.
new.tip: On Sundays it only opens for lunch. Book ahead in summer and on weekends, when the quay is busy.
new.q: Aux Pêcheurs d'Étaples, 3 Boulevard de l'Impératrice, Étaples

new.title: Fill a basket at the Saturday market in Saint-Omer
new.desc: Every Saturday morning, stallholders take over Place Foch and the streets around it, under the town hall. The tourist office calls it a veritable institution, and it is where the market gardeners of the Audomarois marsh, farmed between canals since the Middle Ages, sell their vegetables.
new.tip: It runs from about 8 am to half past noon. Look for marsh-grown cauliflower in season, the crop the area is known for.

new.title: Taste genièvre at the Persyn distillery in Houlle
new.desc: Juniper spirit has been made at this distillery since 1812, and the tourist office describes it as the oldest working grain distillery in France. The visit starts with a film, then goes past the grain, the stills and the oak casks where Houlle genièvre and a whisky age.
new.tip: Tours take around 40 minutes and are best booked by phone beforehand. Locals drink genièvre ice cold, or tip a drop into coffee to make a bistouille.
new.q: Distillerie Persyn, 19 Route de Watten, Houlle

new.title: Buy a Chat Bleu chocolate in Le Touquet
new.desc: Two cat-loving sisters opened this chocolate shop in 1912 and named it after their blue Persians. The house speciality, the Chat Bleu, is praliné held between two sheets of nougatine, and the counters are lined with almond-paste kittens and ladybirds that generations of children have been bought here.
new.tip: The shop on Rue Saint-Jean opens daily but closes over lunch. A small box of Chats Bleus travels well if you need a present.
new.q: Au Chat Bleu, 47 bis Rue Saint-Jean, Le Touquet-Paris-Plage

new.title: Crack a crab at the Fête du Crabe in Audresselles
new.desc: Audresselles is a fishing village built on a dune, with low white houses painted with a band of colour along the base and clinker-built boats called flobarts. On Pentecost weekend it throws its crab festival, when the village's fishing family sells shellfish and fish at the covered market.
new.tip: Pentecost falls in May or June depending on the year. While you are there, walk up to the fortified church of Saint-Jean-Baptiste, which dates from the 12th century.

new.title: Look up at Beffy the dragon on Béthune's belfry
new.desc: The stone belfry of Béthune was begun in 1388 and stands alone in the middle of the Grand'Place. The tower rises 33 metres and carries a 17 metre campanile topped by a dragon weathervane nicknamed Beffy. Shellfire destroyed the top and the carillon in May 1918, and it has been on the UNESCO list with the belfries of Belgium and France since 2005.
new.tip: There are 133 steps to the top. Climbs are organised by the tourist office, so ask there for the times.

new.title: Walk the oldest miners' rows at the Cité des Électriciens
new.desc: Built in 1856 by the Bruay mining company, this is the oldest preserved pit village in northern France: rows of brick terraced houses, each with its own garden, in streets named after pioneers of electricity. It is part of the mining basin listed by UNESCO in 2012 and reopened in 2019 as a cultural site after a restoration led by architect Philippe Prost.
new.tip: Allow time for the gardens as well as the exhibition rooms. The site is in Bruay-la-Buissière, about 15 minutes by car from Béthune.

new.title: Find the upturned boat houses of Équihen-Plage
new.desc: When Équihen was a beaching harbour, poor fishing families took over worn-out boats, turned the hulls upside down and lived under them. These homes were called quilles en l'air, keels in the air. Eight have been rebuilt with modern comforts at the municipal campsite on the cliff, facing the sea.
new.tip: They are let as holiday lodgings, so look from the path and leave the guests in peace. You can also book one and sleep under a keel yourself.
new.q: Camping municipal de la Falaise, Équihen-Plage

new.title: Stand in the roofless nave of Saint-Bertin Abbey
new.desc: The Benedictine abbey of Saint-Bertin was founded in the 7th century under the name Sithiu and grew into one of the great monasteries of the north. Its church was dismantled after the Revolution and its tower, the last part standing, came down in 1947. The ruins have been a listed monument since 1840.
new.tip: The ruins are in the open at the end of Rue Saint-Bertin, an easy walk from the cathedral. Come late in the day, when the light falls through the empty arches.

new.title: Find the lighthouse in the middle of Calais
new.desc: Calais lit this lighthouse in October 1848 and, unusually, built it close to the town centre rather than out on the shore. It is white with a black band under the lantern, was electrified in 1883 and has been a listed monument since 2011. A staircase of 271 steps leads to the lantern.
new.tip: Climbs are run by a local association on certain days, so ask the tourist office before you count on it. Take a windproof layer for the gallery, even in summer.

new.title: Sing Les Corons with the crowd at Stade Bollaert
new.desc: Stade Bollaert-Delelis seats a little over 38,000 people, more than the whole population of Lens. The loudest supporters of RC Lens stand in the Marek, which is a side stand rather than an end behind the goal. At the end of the half-time break the whole ground sings Les Corons, Pierre Bachelet's song about the mining rows.
new.tip: Home games sell out quickly, so buy tickets as soon as they go on sale. Stay in your seat at half-time or you will miss the song.

new.title: Walk to the bird hide at the Romelaëre ponds
new.desc: This national nature reserve covers 104 hectares of old peat diggings that filled with water and turned into ponds and reedbeds, on the edge of the Saint-Omer marsh. Trails dotted with bird hides start at the Grange Nature in Clairmarais, including a stretch of about 2 km adapted for wheelchairs. Around 200 bird species have been recorded here.
new.tip: Entry is free. The reserve shuts for the winter, roughly from mid December to mid March.
new.q: La Grange Nature, Rue du Romelaëre, Clairmarais

new.title: Watch migrating birds at the Platier d'Oye
new.desc: Between Calais and Dunkirk, the Platier d'Oye reserve protects 391 hectares of dunes, wet meadows and foreshore on the left bank of the Aa estuary. It was classified in 1987 because migrating birds stop here in great numbers on their way along the coast.
new.tip: Bring binoculars and something warm, as there is no shelter from the wind. Spring and autumn passage are the busiest times.
new.q: Réserve naturelle nationale du Platier d'Oye, Oye-Plage
